epithet.en: Wife and mother at the summer house

1.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay promises James a trip to the Lighthouse if the weather is fine, and knits a stocking for the lighthouse keeper's sick boy. She scolds her children for mocking the guest Charles Tansley and takes him with her on an errand into town. On the walk he tells her about his poor family, and after she visits a woman in a cottage he is struck by her beauty.

2.modern-en: Tansley tells James there will be no trip to the Lighthouse, trying awkwardly to sound kind for her sake. Mrs. Ramsay privately calls him an odious little man for saying it again.

3.modern-en: She comforts James, telling him it may be fine after all, and helps him cut pictures from a catalogue. When the men's voices stop she feels a moment of dread, then is soothed by her husband's chanting. Seeing Lily at her easel, she remembers she is supposed to hold her pose for Lily's picture.

4.modern-en: Lily, painting, has Mrs. Ramsay and James in the window as her subject. Lily secretly longs to throw herself at Mrs. Ramsay's knee and tell her what she feels, and thinks Mr. Ramsay wears his wife out.

5.modern-en: Measuring the stocking against James's leg, Mrs. Ramsay decides it is too short. She suddenly thinks William Bankes and Lily should marry, and frets about the shabby house and the Swiss maid whose father is dying. The narrative dwells on her famous beauty and on what, if anything, lies behind it.

6.modern-en: After her husband's embarrassing outburst she quietly soothes James. When Mr. Ramsay insists there is no chance of fine weather and curses her for raising false hopes, she is stung by his harshness. He then humbly offers to ask the coastguards, and she feels she reveres no one more.

7.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay comes to her insisting he is a failure, and she pours out sympathy and reassurance until he is restored. Afterwards she is exhausted and uneasy: she dislikes people thinking he depends on her, and dislikes hiding small worries from him, like the fifty-pound greenhouse roof.

8.modern-en: Mr. Carmichael's coolness makes her wonder whether her urge to help people is secretly vanity. She goes back to reading the fairy tale of the Fisherman and his Wife to James.

9.modern-en: Lily remembers a night when Mrs. Ramsay came to her room and insisted that every woman must marry, and how she laid her head in Mrs. Ramsay's lap, longing to know her secret heart. Mr. Bankes gazes at her with silent rapture as she reads to James.

10.modern-en: She sends Cam with a message to Mildred and finishes the fairy tale for James, while wondering whether Minta has accepted Paul and whether the late walkers are safe. She wishes James and Cam would never grow up and thinks of life as an enemy she must bargain with. When the Lighthouse beam appears, she knows James will remember his disappointment all his life.

11.modern-en: Alone at last, she sinks into a private stillness and feels herself become the Lighthouse's long third stroke. She catches herself thinking "We are in the hands of the Lord" and rejects it as a lie. Sensing that her husband wants to protect her, she takes the green shawl and goes out to him.

12.modern-en: Walking in the garden with Mr. Ramsay, she talks about the gardener, Jasper's shooting, Tansley and Andrew's scholarship, avoiding the subject of money. They share an awkward, tender moment when he kisses her hand. Seeing Lily and William Bankes strolling together, she is sure they must marry.

13.modern-en: With her husband she watches Prue and Jasper throwing catches, and greets Lily and Mr. Bankes by saying she has "triumphed" in getting Bankes to dinner. She asks Prue whether Nancy went with the walkers.

14.modern-en: Walking home after proposing to Minta, Paul thinks it was Mrs. Ramsay who made him believe he could do anything. He plans to go straight to her and say he has done it, thanks to her.

15.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay has asked whether Nancy went with the walkers. Prue answers that she thinks Nancy did.

16.modern-en: While Jasper and Rose choose her jewels, she frets about the late walkers and the Bœuf en Daube. When she hears them come in, she goes down to dinner like a queen receiving her people.

17.modern-en: At the head of the table she first feels cut off from everything, then gathers the scattered guests together, silently asks Lily to help her with Tansley, and senses that Paul and Minta are engaged. As the candles are lit she feels a moment of peace she believes will last forever. She leaves the room while her husband and Mr. Carmichael recite a poem.

18.modern-en: Upstairs she finds Cam and James awake and frightened of a boar's skull, wraps it in her shawl, and soothes Cam to sleep. She promises James they will go to the Lighthouse on the next fine day. Coming down, she lets the young people go to the beach and joins her husband.

19.modern-en: Reading beside her husband, she finds calm in a sonnet and tells him Paul and Minta are engaged. She cannot bring herself to say she loves him, but she smiles and says he was right that it will be wet tomorrow, and he understands.

22.modern-en: A short bracketed passage reports that Mrs. Ramsay died suddenly one night. The next morning Mr. Ramsay stretches out his arms for her in a dark passage, and they stay empty.

27.modern-en: Cleaning the long-empty house, Mrs. McNab fingers Mrs. Ramsay's old gray gardening cloak and remembers her kindness. She has heard that Mrs. Ramsay died years ago in London, very suddenly at the end.

28.modern-en: Mrs. McNab's memory of the lady in the gray cloak has faded like a patch of sunlight on the wall. Over tea during the cleaning, she half remembers the family's busy days, when the house was full of guests.

30.modern-en: Back at the house after ten years, Lily finds she feels almost nothing about Mrs. Ramsay's death. Then she grows angry with her for giving and giving until she died, leaving all this behind. She decides to finish the picture she began of her.

31.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay tells Lily that his wife used to send things to the Lighthouse men, one reason he wants to make the trip. Lily remembers the look of rapturous sympathy she saw on Mrs. Ramsay's face and can't imitate it.

32.modern-en: As she paints, Lily remembers a windy day on the beach when Mrs. Ramsay wrote letters while Lily and Charles Tansley skipped stones. She realizes how Mrs. Ramsay could make a moment permanent ("Life stand still here"), and feels she owes her a revelation.

33.modern-en: In the boat Mr. Ramsay thinks of his wife as vague about facts, like all women. James half-remembers a moment when his mother, sitting in a low chair, laughed and gave in to his father.

34.modern-en: Lily imagines telling Mrs. Ramsay how the Rayleys' marriage turned out, and feels she has triumphed over her mania for marriage. Then grief suddenly overwhelms her, and she cries out Mrs. Ramsay's name.

36.modern-en: Lily's pain eases into a sense of Mrs. Ramsay near her. She recalls how, after hearing of her death, she kept picturing her crossing fields with a wreath of white flowers.

37.modern-en: James remembers his mother as the one person who spoke the truth and to whom he could say anything. He recalls how she went stiff and left him when his father interrupted them.

40.modern-en: Lily thinks about Mrs. Ramsay's errands to the poor, Mr. Carmichael's dislike of her, and the storms and reconciliations of her marriage. At last Lily seems to see her sitting in the chair by the window, knitting, casting her shadow on the step.

1.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay tells James flatly that the weather won't be fine for the Lighthouse trip, and his son would kill him if he could. He prides himself on never softening an unpleasant fact, and paces the terrace with his admirer Charles Tansley.

3.modern-en: Pacing the terrace, he half-sings, half-shouts lines from a poem about a cavalry charge. Mrs. Ramsay turns anxiously to see whether anyone has heard him, and is relieved that only Lily is near.

4.modern-en: Declaiming "Someone had blundered," he almost knocks over Lily's easel and then runs straight into Lily and Mr. Bankes, ashamed to be caught. Bankes thinks their friendship faded after Ramsay married and that he did his best work before forty; Lily weighs his vanity and tyranny against his fiery unworldliness.

6.modern-en: Shaken at being seen, he recovers, then snaps that there is no chance of going to the Lighthouse and curses his wife for raising false hopes, before humbly offering to ask the coastguards. On the terrace he struggles to get past "Q" in his thinking and fears he is a failure, then takes comfort in the sight of his wife and son.

7.modern-en: He comes to Mrs. Ramsay insisting that he is a failure and demanding sympathy. Once she has reassured him he goes off, renewed, to watch the children play cricket.

8.modern-en: Walking, he muses on Shakespeare and the ordinary man and on lectures he will give at Cardiff. Standing alone at the edge of the lawn facing the sea, he inspires reverence, while Lily and Mr. Bankes wonder why so brave a thinker needs so much praise.

9.modern-en: Mr. Bankes wishes Ramsay could behave more like other people and calls him "a bit of a hypocrite". Lily thinks him the most sincere of men, but also tyrannical and unjust.

11.modern-en: Passing his wife, he sees the sternness in her face and is saddened that he can't protect her or reach her. She comes out to him.

12.modern-en: Walking in the garden with Mrs. Ramsay, he discusses Tansley, Prue's looks and Andrew's scholarship. He daydreams about solitary walks but reminds himself he is the father of eight, and kisses her hand.

13.modern-en: He stands with his wife watching Prue and Jasper throw catches, a picture of marriage in Lily's eyes. Then he goes off to his study chuckling over a story about the philosopher Hume stuck in a bog.

17.modern-en: At dinner he nearly explodes when Mr. Carmichael asks for another plate of soup, teases Minta, and grows uneasy when the talk turns to whether books last. Afterwards he recites the poem "Luriana, Lurilee".

19.modern-en: Reading a Scott novel, he is moved to tears and reassured about his own worth. He wants his wife to tell him she loves him; instead she says he was right about the weather, and he understands.

22.modern-en: In a bracketed passage, he stumbles along a dark passage one morning and stretches out his arms for his wife, who died suddenly the night before. His arms stay empty.

28.modern-en: Mrs. McNab remembers the lean old gentleman talking to himself on the lawn. She isn't sure whether he is still alive.

30.modern-en: Ten years later he is back at the house, determined to sail to the Lighthouse with Cam and James, and loses his temper at the delays. Pacing the terrace and muttering "Alone" and "Perished", he looks to Lily for something she dreads giving.

31.modern-en: He presses Lily for sympathy, sighing about his wife and the painful expedition; she can say nothing until she praises his boots, which delights him. He shows her his own way of tying a knot, then leads Cam and James down to the boat.

32.modern-en: From the lawn, Lily watches his boat hoist its sail and set out across the bay. She decides he must be sitting in that distant, silent boat with Cam and James.

33.modern-en: Once the boat is moving he is content, chatting with old Macalister about a storm and quoting lines about perishing alone. He tries to win Cam over by asking who is looking after the puppy.

34.modern-en: Lily reflects that she never managed to praise him to his face. She remembers how gallant he was with Minta, picking her flowers and lending her books.

36.modern-en: Lily spots his boat halfway across the bay. She thinks of him as a very old man who marched past her with a brown paper parcel, asking for sympathy she refused.

37.modern-en: He reads in the becalmed boat while James broods on killing the "tyranny" in him. When the wind returns he raises his hand as if conducting music.

39.modern-en: Cam watches him reading his little book and remembers him writing in his study among the old gentlemen. There he seemed most lovable and wise, gently asking if there was anything he could give her.

40.modern-en: Lily's feeling for him changes as the boat gets further away. She remembers the quarrels and reconciliations of his marriage, and at the end she finds she wants him.

41.modern-en: Nearing the Lighthouse, he finishes his book, shares out lunch, and tells Macalister he is seventy-one. He praises James's steering ("Well done!") and springs onto the rock with his parcel like a young man.

42.modern-en: Lily senses that he has landed at the Lighthouse. She feels she has finally given him what she wanted to give him that morning.

epithet.en: Painter and guest of the Ramsays

3.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay notices Lily painting at the edge of the lawn and remembers she is supposed to keep still for the picture. She thinks Lily will never marry but likes her independence.

4.modern-en: Lily dreads anyone seeing her picture but lets William Bankes stand beside her, and they walk down to look at the bay. Under a pear tree she weighs Bankes's goodness against Mr. Ramsay's greatness and faults, and feels she is in love with the Ramsays' whole world.

5.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay suddenly decides that Lily and William Bankes should marry. She thinks Lily's charm is her slanting "Chinese eyes", which only a clever man would notice.

6.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay, lost in reciting a cavalry charge, has blundered straight into Lily and William Bankes. The collision shatters his heroic mood.

8.modern-en: Putting away her paints, Lily suggests that Mrs. Ramsay gives her husband what he asks for too easily. She thinks the change from his books to the family's games must be upsetting for him.

9.modern-en: Discussing Mr. Ramsay with Bankes, Lily remembers resting her head on Mrs. Ramsay's knee and longing to be one with her. Bankes studies her canvas; she explains the purple triangle as Mrs. Ramsay and James, and feels something intimate has been shared.

10.modern-en: Cam races past Lily's easel without stopping for her or Mr. Bankes. Mrs. Ramsay has to call her back twice.

12.modern-en: Walking in the garden with her husband, Mrs. Ramsay sees Lily strolling with William Bankes. She is sure they must marry.

13.modern-en: Lily walks with Bankes as he talks about his travels and the great painters, and says she will always go on painting. Seeing Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay watching their children, she sees them for a moment as a picture of marriage itself.

17.modern-en: At dinner she decides to move the tree to the middle of her picture and marks the spot with the salt cellar. At Mrs. Ramsay's silent request she is kind to Tansley against her will. She asks to help Paul hunt for the brooch, is scorched by his laugh, and is thankful she need not marry.

18.modern-en: Lily watches Mrs. Ramsay slip away after dinner, and the party drifts apart once she has gone. Then she sees her on the stairs as the young people plan a trip to the beach.

20.modern-en: Coming in from outside with the others, Lily asks whether to leave the hall light burning. Prue says no, not if everyone is in.

28.modern-en: A bracketed note reports that Lily has her bag carried up to the house late one September evening. Mr. Carmichael arrives by the same train.

29.modern-en: Tired from traveling, Lily falls asleep in the house to the sound of the sea. At dawn she wakes with a start and sits up in bed: here she is again.

30.modern-en: At breakfast, back after ten years, Lily finds she feels almost nothing about Mrs. Ramsay's death. She remembers her unfinished picture and sets up her easel, but Mr. Ramsay's demanding presence stops her painting. At forty-four she is angry with Mrs. Ramsay for having died.

31.modern-en: She can't give Mr. Ramsay the sympathy he demands and ends up praising his boots. When he leaves, her sympathy rises, too late to give.

32.modern-en: She makes her first strokes on the canvas and remembers Charles Tansley and Mrs. Ramsay on the beach. She watches the boat set sail.

34.modern-en: Painting, she pieces together the story of the Rayleys' troubled marriage and remembers her close friendship with William Bankes. Grief for Mrs. Ramsay suddenly overwhelms her, and she cries out her name.

36.modern-en: Her pain eases into a sense of Mrs. Ramsay beside her, and she goes back to the problem of the hedge. She spots Mr. Ramsay's boat halfway across the bay.

38.modern-en: Lily stands looking out at the calm bay. The boat seems to have been swallowed up by distance, and only the smoke of a steamer hangs in the air.

40.modern-en: She thinks about Mr. Carmichael, Charles Tansley and the Ramsays' marriage. Then she seems to see Mrs. Ramsay sitting in the window, knitting, and wants to share it with Mr. Ramsay.

42.modern-en: Lily senses that Mr. Ramsay has landed, and Mr. Carmichael, standing beside her, says the same. She draws a line in the center of her canvas and finishes: "I have had my vision."

1.modern-en: Six-year-old James is thrilled at the thought of going to the Lighthouse, then furious when his father says the weather won't allow it. He cuts pictures out of a catalogue at his mother's feet.

2.modern-en: Tansley tells James there will be no trip to the Lighthouse. He tries to soften his voice for Mrs. Ramsay's sake, but only annoys her.

3.modern-en: His mother strokes his hair and tells him he may wake to find the sun shining. She helps him look through the catalogue for a picture that will need careful cutting out.

4.modern-en: From her easel Lily studies Mrs. Ramsay sitting in the window with James. Mr. Bankes privately nicknames him "James the Ruthless".

5.modern-en: His mother measures the stocking for the lighthouse keeper's boy against James's leg. Jealous, he fidgets on purpose until her sharp tone makes him stand still.

6.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay tickles his bare leg with a sprig and jokes that James will have to write his own dissertation one day. James brushes the sprig away, hating his father.

7.modern-en: James hates his father for interrupting and for his egotism and grand gestures. Standing stiffly between his mother's knees, he feels her strength being drained by his father's demand for sympathy.

8.modern-en: His mother reads him the fairy tale of the Fisherman and his Wife. She thinks he is the most sensitive of her children.

9.modern-en: Lily's picture shows Mrs. Ramsay reading to James as a purple triangle. She wonders whether a figure such as James could fill the empty foreground.

10.modern-en: His mother finishes the story, and James gazes at the Lighthouse beam. Mildred carries him off to bed, still looking back.

18.modern-en: He can't sleep because of the boar's skull on the nursery wall but won't let anyone remove it. His mother covers it and promises they'll go to the Lighthouse on the next fine day.

30.modern-en: Now sixteen, James scowls at the lamp when his father tells Lily she will find them much changed. He doggedly says yes when his father demands to know whether they want to go to the Lighthouse.

31.modern-en: He and Cam come out onto the terrace late, lagging side by side like a serious, melancholy couple. They follow their father down the path to the boat.

32.modern-en: Lily remembers Mrs. Ramsay sitting on the step with James. She watches the distant boat carrying him, Cam and their father set sail.

33.modern-en: Steering the boat, James and Cam have vowed to resist their father's tyranny. James watches Cam, fearing she will give in, and half-remembers his mother surrendering to his father.

37.modern-en: Becalmed, James broods on striking to the heart the "tyranny" he sees in his father, and remembers his mother as the one person he could say anything to. He compares the stark real Lighthouse with the misty tower of his childhood and decides both are the Lighthouse.

39.modern-en: James keeps his eye on the sail. Cam imagines him calling their father a sarcastic brute, an egotist and a tyrant.

41.modern-en: The stark tower satisfies James. When his father says "Well done!" about his steering, he is quietly delighted.

4.modern-en: Cam, the Ramsays' youngest daughter, is picking flowers on the bank. She fiercely refuses to give one to Mr. Bankes, stamping and clenching her fist.

9.modern-en: As Lily snaps her paintbox shut, "that wild villain" Cam dashes past. The moment seems to fix the scene in Lily's mind.

10.modern-en: Cam races past everyone until her mother calls her back and sends her with a message to Mildred. She repeats Mildred's answer in a sing-song.

17.modern-en: Cam is not at dinner. Mr. Bankes supposes that she, his favorite of the children, is in bed.

18.modern-en: Cam can't sleep because the boar's skull on the nursery wall throws horned shadows. Her mother wraps it in her shawl and talks her to sleep with a story of mountains, gardens and antelopes.

30.modern-en: Now about seventeen, Cam twists her handkerchief round her finger as her father speaks to the family. She stumbles wretchedly into agreeing to go to the Lighthouse.

31.modern-en: She and James come out late and lag side by side like a serious, melancholy couple. Her father sends her for a cloak before they follow him down to the boat.

32.modern-en: Lily watches the distant boat in which Cam, James and their father are setting out. It moves slowly past the other boats and out to sea.

33.modern-en: Cam has joined James's pact against their father, but she is drawn to him. She can't pick out their house on shore, and answers "Jasper" when he asks who is looking after the puppy.

37.modern-en: Cam trails her hand in the water, imagining an underwater world of pearls and green light. Then the wind drops and the boat lies becalmed in the hot sun.

39.modern-en: Seeing the island from the sea for the first time, Cam feels a sudden rush of joy at the adventure. She remembers her father writing in his study, gentle and wise, and feels safe with him.

41.modern-en: Sleepy but happy, Cam eats lunch in the boat. She sees how pleased James is when their father praises him.

epithet.en: Botanist and old friend of Mr. Ramsay

4.modern-en: William Bankes, an old friend of Mr. Ramsay's, joins Lily at her easel and walks with her to the bay. He thinks about how their friendship faded after Ramsay married, and says Ramsay did his best work before forty. Lily admires his goodness.

5.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay decides Bankes should marry Lily. We learn how moved he once was by Mrs. Ramsay's beauty, even over the telephone.

6.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay, reciting a poem about a cavalry charge, has blundered straight into Lily and Bankes. The encounter shatters his heroic mood.

7.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay suspects that her husband's last book was not quite his best. She has gathered this from William Bankes, and is afraid her husband might guess.

8.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay inspires in Bankes an intermittent reverence. But Bankes, like Lily, finds his need for praise and his concealments pitiable.

9.modern-en: Bankes calls Ramsay "a bit of a hypocrite" and gazes at Mrs. Ramsay in silent rapture. He examines Lily's canvas with serious scientific interest.

10.modern-en: Bankes, who would have liked a daughter of his own, holds out his hand to Cam. She races past without stopping.

12.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay sees Bankes and Lily walking together in the dusk. She decides they must marry.

13.modern-en: Strolling with Lily, he tells her about the pictures he has seen in Amsterdam, Madrid and Rome, and mentions his wife's long ill health. For once he has agreed to dine with the Ramsays.

16.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay wants dinner to be especially good because William Bankes has at last agreed to dine with them. The Bœuf en Daube must not be spoiled.

17.modern-en: At dinner he secretly feels he doesn't enjoy family life, then warms to Mrs. Ramsay over the Bœuf en Daube. He argues politics with Tansley and praises the Waverley novels.

18.modern-en: After dinner he takes Tansley by the arm and goes out to the terrace to finish their political argument. Lily feels the evening's balance shift from poetry to politics.

20.modern-en: He comes in from the terrace, saying they must wait for the future to show. The house then settles for the night.

31.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay recalls that there was once talk of Lily marrying Bankes. Nothing came of it.

34.modern-en: Lily remembers their long friendship and summer outings to Hampton Court, where he talked about perspective and architecture. She realizes that she loves William Bankes.

39.modern-en: Cam remembers old gentlemen, perhaps Mr. Carmichael or Mr. Bankes, reading The Times with her father in the study. They would say something brief now and then.

epithet.en: Young academic and admirer of Mr. Ramsay

1.modern-en: Charles Tansley, a young admirer of Mr. Ramsay, confirms the wind is wrong for the Lighthouse, and the children mock him as "the little atheist". Walking into town with Mrs. Ramsay, he tells her about his poor family and falls under the spell of her beauty.

2.modern-en: He tells James there will be no trip to the Lighthouse. He is trying to soften his voice for Mrs. Ramsay's sake, but she only finds him odious.

3.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay is annoyed that he rubbed in her husband's bad news to James. When the men's voices stop, she concludes he has been dismissed and does not mind.

6.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay teases her husband for sending "that poor young man" away. Mr. Ramsay says Tansley has gone in to write his dissertation.

7.modern-en: When Mr. Ramsay insists he is a failure, Mrs. Ramsay replies that Charles Tansley thinks him the greatest metaphysician of the time. It is not enough for him.

8.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay's lonely stand at the edge of the lawn inspires reverence in those around him. In Tansley it is an obsequious reverence.

9.modern-en: Looking at her unsatisfactory picture, Lily hears Tansley whispering that women can't paint and women can't write. Mrs. Ramsay, she remembers, liked to act out Tansley losing his umbrella.

10.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay remembers Tansley sniggering when she told Paul and Minta there wasn't a cloud for miles. She would much rather have a kindly booby than a clever man writing dissertations.

12.modern-en: Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay discuss Tansley and his dissertation, which is all he has to count on. Mrs. Ramsay hopes he won't fall in love with Prue.

17.modern-en: At dinner Tansley feels out of place and scornful of the Ramsays' chatter. Lily teases him and then, at Mrs. Ramsay's silent request, draws him out. He argues politics with Bankes and attacks the Waverley novels.

18.modern-en: After dinner he goes out to the terrace with Mr. Bankes to talk politics. Upstairs, Mrs. Ramsay worries he'll wake the children by knocking books off his table.

19.modern-en: Tansley's remark at dinner that people don't read Scott any more has sent Mr. Ramsay off to read a Scott novel. Mrs. Ramsay knows her husband fears the same will be said of him.

32.modern-en: Lily remembers Tansley standing close behind her saying women can't paint, and boasting of his cheap tobacco. She also remembers a happy afternoon on the beach when they skipped stones while Mrs. Ramsay wrote letters.

34.modern-en: Lily remembers the beach again, with Charles sending stones skipping over the waves. Mrs. Ramsay sat nearby, silent, looking out to sea.

40.modern-en: Lily reflects that Tansley has got his fellowship, married, and lives at Golders Green. She remembers hearing him preach brotherly love from a platform during the war.

epithet.en: Elderly poet staying with the Ramsays

1.modern-en: Augustus Carmichael lies drowsing on the lawn when Mrs. Ramsay asks if he wants anything from town. She tells Tansley he might have been a great philosopher but made an unfortunate marriage.

7.modern-en: Just as Mrs. Ramsay is feeling uneasy about her marriage, Augustus Carmichael shuffles past in his yellow slippers. Some demon makes her call out to ask if he is going indoors.

8.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay feels he doesn't trust her, which she blames on his wife, and wonders whether her wish to help is vanity. The children say he takes opium.

9.modern-en: Lily remembers Mrs. Ramsay coming to her room late at night and acting out the day's comedies. One of them was Mr. Carmichael snuffling and sniffing.

11.modern-en: Alone, Mrs. Ramsay thinks that everyone has unseen depths beneath the surface. She includes Augustus Carmichael among them.

12.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay says he has had about enough of Bankes and of Carmichael. He would like a little solitude.

17.modern-en: At dinner he asks for a second plate of soup, which infuriates Mr. Ramsay. Mrs. Ramsay admires his calm and his devotion to Andrew. After dinner he rises and chants "Luriana, Lurilee", bowing to her as if in homage.

20.modern-en: As the house goes to bed, all the lamps are put out except Mr. Carmichael's. He keeps his candle burning to read Virgil.

21.modern-en: Darkness floods the house. In a bracketed note, Mr. Carmichael blows out his candle; it is past midnight.

25.modern-en: A bracketed note reports that Mr. Carmichael has published a book of poems that spring. It has had an unexpected success, which people put down to the war reviving interest in poetry.

28.modern-en: A bracketed note reports that he arrives at the restored house by the same train as Lily Briscoe. It is late one evening in September.

29.modern-en: Back in the full house, he reads by candlelight while Lily sleeps. Shutting his book, he thinks it all looks much as it used to years ago.

30.modern-en: He pads in for his coffee and takes it out to sit in the sun. Lily sets up her easel near him for protection.

31.modern-en: He lies contentedly in a deck chair reading a French novel. Lily wishes he were closer, so that a man could stem Mr. Ramsay's flood of self-pity.

32.modern-en: Lily paints near Mr. Carmichael on the lawn and half wishes she could simply talk to him. As she works, she loses track of whether he is there or not.

34.modern-en: Lily wants to ask him whether he remembers the old days, and what everything means. She has a curious feeling that he hears what she cannot say.

36.modern-en: Lily cries out Mrs. Ramsay's name, but the old man does not hear her. He stays calm and benign in his chair.

39.modern-en: Cam remembers old gentlemen, perhaps Mr. Carmichael or Mr. Bankes, reading The Times with her father in the study. In their company she felt free to think whatever she liked.

40.modern-en: Lily reflects that he has become famous for his poetry, and that he was said to have lost all interest in life when Andrew died. She thinks he never much liked Mrs. Ramsay.

42.modern-en: When Lily says aloud that Mr. Ramsay has landed, he rises and stands beside her, saying, "They will have landed." She feels they have been thinking the same things all along.

1.modern-en: Minta Doyle is one of the guests staying with the Ramsays. She has gone out with the others when Mrs. Ramsay invites Tansley to town.

4.modern-en: Lily would hide her canvas from Minta Doyle, as from almost anyone. Mr. Bankes thinks Lily has more good sense than the more alluring Miss Doyle.

9.modern-en: Lily remembers Mrs. Ramsay coming to her room late at night. She insisted that Lily, Minta, all of them must marry.

10.modern-en: Minta has gone for a walk with Paul Rayley, and Mrs. Ramsay waits to learn whether she has accepted him. Mrs. Ramsay wonders how Minta's parents, whom she calls the Owl and the Poker, produced such a tomboy daughter.

14.modern-en: On the walk Minta sings, holds Nancy's hand, and is terrified of bulls and of being cut off by the tide. She loses her grandmother's brooch and cries. Paul, who has just asked her to marry him, comforts her.

16.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay is annoyed that Minta and the others are late on the night of her special dinner. At last she hears them come in.

17.modern-en: Minta sits beside Mr. Ramsay, glowing with her "golden haze", and he teases her. Mrs. Ramsay realizes she and Paul are engaged and feels a pang of jealousy at her husband's delight in her.

18.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay takes Minta's arm as they leave dinner and thinks of "the Rayleys" carrying on her world. Minta tells her Paul has a watch as the young people set off for the beach.

19.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay tells her husband that Paul and Minta are engaged. He thinks, as he always does, that the girl is much too good for the young man.

34.modern-en: Lily pieces together the Rayleys' marriage: after a year or so it went badly, with bitter scenes, but it has since settled into friendship. Minta once walked ahead of Lily and Bankes with a hole in her stocking.

40.modern-en: Lily remembers Minta, Paul and William Bankes at Mrs. Ramsay's side during her rigid silences with her husband. Once the couple went off to make it up, the young people hid their discomfort by picking flowers and chattering.

1.modern-en: Paul Rayley is one of the guests staying with the Ramsays. He has gone out with the others when Mrs. Ramsay invites Tansley to town.

4.modern-en: Lily would hide her canvas from Paul Rayley, as from almost anyone. Only William Bankes may watch her paint.

10.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay waits to hear whether Paul has proposed to Minta on their walk. Her sympathies are with him; she thinks him a good fellow, if not brilliant.

14.modern-en: On the walk Paul asks Minta to marry him, and it is the worst moment of his life. When she loses her brooch he vows to slip out at dawn to find it, and he walks home thinking he owes his courage to Mrs. Ramsay.

16.modern-en: He comes back to the house late with the others. As Mrs. Ramsay passes through the hall, he stands stiffly, not moving a muscle.

17.modern-en: At dinner Mrs. Ramsay knows from his "we" that he and Minta are engaged. He tells Lily he'll look for the brooch at dawn and laughs off her offer to help, and he talks to Mrs. Ramsay about Tolstoy.

18.modern-en: He shows Mrs. Ramsay his gold watch in its wash-leather case, silently thanking her for his engagement. She thinks how lucky Minta is.

19.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay tells her husband Paul and Minta are engaged. She jokes about how nice it must be to marry a man with a wash-leather bag for his watch.

34.modern-en: Lily imagines the Rayleys' marriage: bitter scenes on the stairs, and Paul playing chess in coffeehouses. Later he took up with another woman, which oddly steadied the marriage.

40.modern-en: Lily remembers meeting Paul on the stairs after Mr. Ramsay, finding an earwig in his milk, sent it flying onto the terrace. The two of them laughed like children.

1.modern-en: Prue is one of the Ramsay children who mock Tansley. At table she and her sisters honor their mother's severity while privately dreaming of a different life.

4.modern-en: Mr. Bankes privately nicknames her "Prue the Fair". He thinks she is bound to be beautiful.

10.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay thinks of Prue as an angel with the younger children. At night especially, her beauty is starting to take one's breath away.

12.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay says Prue will be more beautiful than she is; Mr. Ramsay can't see it. She tells him to look tonight.

13.modern-en: Prue throws catches with Jasper in the dusk and catches a high ball brilliantly. Her mother draws her back into family life by asking whether Nancy went with the walkers.

15.modern-en: Prue answers her mother's question in her considering way. She thinks Nancy did go with the walkers.

17.modern-en: At dinner Prue watches Minta shyly, beginning to glow with a sense of love. Her mother promises silently that she will be even happier one day.

18.modern-en: Seeing her mother on the stairs, Prue thinks there is no one else like her and feels like a child again. She asks whether they may go down to the beach to watch the waves.

20.modern-en: Coming in from the dark, Prue says one can hardly tell sea from land. She tells Andrew to put out the light in the hall.

25.modern-en: A bracketed note reports that Prue was given in marriage, on her father's arm, one May; people said she looked beautiful. Another reports that she died that summer of an illness connected with childbirth.

27.modern-en: Mrs. McNab has heard that Miss Prue died with her first baby. Everyone, she thinks, has lost someone in these years.

30.modern-en: Sitting at breakfast, Lily repeats to herself that Mrs. Ramsay is dead, Andrew killed, and Prue dead too. The words rouse no feeling in her.

40.modern-en: Lily remembers how Prue went white and anxious during her parents' quarrels, and how her mother seemed to promise her the same happiness one day. Prue enjoyed that happiness for less than a year.

1.modern-en: Andrew is one of the Ramsay children who mock Tansley. He calls him a sarcastic brute.

4.modern-en: Mr. Bankes nicknames him "Andrew the Just", credited with brains. Lily remembers Andrew explaining his father's philosophy to her: "Think of a kitchen table when you're not there."

5.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay remembers Andrew saying the shabby chairs had their insides all over the floor. If he wants to dissect crabs, she can't stop him.

10.modern-en: Andrew has gone with Paul and Minta, carrying his crab net, and his mother worries he'll be cut off by the tide. She notes that even her husband thinks his gift for mathematics is extraordinary.

12.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay wishes Andrew would work harder, or he will lose his chance of a scholarship. Mrs. Ramsay would be proud of him either way, and her husband tells her not to worry about his being late.

14.modern-en: On the walk Andrew admires Minta as a walker but thinks her reckless, then goes off crab-hunting. He finds the fuss over the lost brooch undignified.

17.modern-en: At dinner his mother tells him to hold his plate lower. He is first to laugh at her lecture on the English dairy system.

20.modern-en: Andrew comes up from the beach, saying it is almost too dark to see. Prue asks him to put out the hall light.

25.modern-en: A bracketed note reports that a shell killed twenty or thirty young men in France during the war. Andrew Ramsay was among them; his death was instantaneous.

27.modern-en: Mrs. McNab has heard that Mr. Andrew was killed. She reflects that many families have lost their dearest.

30.modern-en: Sitting at breakfast, Lily repeats to herself that Andrew was killed. It rouses no feeling in her.

31.modern-en: Thinking of Mr. Ramsay's philosophy, Lily remembers the kitchen table Andrew once gave her as its symbol. She recalls that Andrew was killed instantly by a shell splinter.

40.modern-en: Lily remembers that Andrew should have been a great mathematician. Mr. Carmichael was said to have lost all interest in life when he died.

1.modern-en: Nancy complains that Tansley followed them all the way to the Hebrides. Her mother sternly corrects her: he was invited.

10.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay can't remember whether Nancy went on the walk with Paul and Minta. She tries to picture them leaving but can't count them.

13.modern-en: Watching Prue catch the ball, Mrs. Ramsay asks her whether Nancy went with the walkers. She is still anxious about them.

14.modern-en: Nancy reluctantly joins the walk when Minta asks her with a dumb look, and broods alone over a rock pool on the beach. Running back, she stumbles on Paul and Minta in each other's arms, which outrages her.

15.modern-en: Prue answers her mother's question. She thinks Nancy did go with them.

16.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay wonders whether Nancy's being with the walkers makes an engagement more or less likely. It makes it less likely, she irrationally feels.

30.modern-en: Ten years later, Nancy has forgotten to order the sandwiches for the Lighthouse trip. She bursts in and asks Lily, half dazed, what one sends to the Lighthouse.

41.modern-en: Mr. Ramsay holds the large, badly packed parcel that Nancy got ready. It is meant for the men at the Lighthouse.

1.modern-en: Jasper is one of the Ramsay children who mock Tansley. Like the others, he sits at table under his mother's eye.

4.modern-en: Jasper strolls past swinging Lily's hand, off to shoot birds. His shot scatters a flock of starlings over the terrace.

10.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay doesn't like Jasper shooting birds. She tells herself it is only a stage.

12.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay worries about Jasper shooting birds. Her husband says it is natural in a boy and he will find better amusements.

13.modern-en: Jasper throws catches with Prue as the light fades. Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay stand watching them.

16.modern-en: Jasper and Rose help their mother choose her jewels, and he gives her his arm going down to dinner. She scolds him for wanting to shoot the rooks she calls Joseph and Mary.

17.modern-en: Jasper sits at dinner in a row with Rose, Prue and Andrew. They share some private joke their mother can't guess.

33.modern-en: In the boat, Mr. Ramsay asks who is looking after the puppy. Cam sullenly answers that Jasper is.

40.modern-en: Lily is glad she need not greet old Mrs. Beckwith with the usual chatter. It would include telling her that Jasper has hidden the chairs.

1.modern-en: Rose is one of the Ramsay children who mock Tansley. She says that no one could possibly like his tie.

5.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay thinks of Rose's collections of shells, reeds and stones cluttering the house. Her children are gifted, she thinks, but in very different ways.

10.modern-en: Mrs. Ramsay thinks Rose's mouth is too big but that she has a wonderful gift with her hands. She makes the dresses for charades and loves arranging tables and flowers.

16.modern-en: Rose helps choose her mother's necklace, a nightly ritual she loves. Mrs. Ramsay senses Rose's deep feeling for her and fears she will suffer.

17.modern-en: Rose has arranged the dish of fruit that delights Mrs. Ramsay at dinner. She nearly bursts out laughing at her father's anger over the soup.

epithet.en: Caretaker of the empty summer house

23.modern-en: Mrs. McNab, an old local woman, comes as directed to the empty house. She tears through its silence to open the windows and dust the bedrooms.

24.modern-en: Nearly seventy, worn and toothless, she lurches from room to room singing an old music-hall song. She has known a hard life but keeps on drinking and gossiping.

25.modern-en: As summer comes, the empty rooms fill with flies and yellow haze. Mrs. McNab lurches about in them, dusting and sweeping.

27.modern-en: Hearing that the house may be sold, she picks flowers to take home and fingers Mrs. Ramsay's old gray cloak, remembering her kindness. She has heard that Mrs. Ramsay, Andrew and Prue are dead; overwhelmed by the damp and decay, she locks up and leaves.

28.modern-en: Summoned by a letter saying the family may come for the summer, she and Mrs. Bast clean and restore the house. Over tea she remembers the old days, the cook, and the old gentleman talking to himself on the lawn.

33.modern-en: Old Macalister sails the Ramsays toward the Lighthouse. He tells Mr. Ramsay about the great storm last Christmas, when ships were wrecked in the bay and the lifeboat went out.

37.modern-en: Macalister's fishing line hangs straight down while the boat lies becalmed. James imagines his father chatting with the Macalisters.

41.modern-en: He praises James's steering and tells Mr. Ramsay he is seventy-five and has never seen a doctor. He points out where three men drowned in the storm.
